common_name: Oliver Loquat (Historic Sweet Orange-Fleshed Gulf Coast Loquat)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Oliver is an old, once widely favored loquat selection still popular with Gulf Coast dooryard growers for its dependable sweetness and small manageable size.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, siting the tree where late-winter blooms and developing spring fruit are shielded from the coldest north winds. Oliver produces medium to large, orange-skinned fruit with pale orange flesh that is notably sweet and carries only one or two seeds per fruit, making it an easy, low-waste loquat for fresh eating. It grows as a compact small to medium tree, generally topping out shorter and denser than many other loquat cultivars, which suits it to smaller dooryard plantings along the Gulf Coast. Fruit ripens over a relatively short window from March into May; thin heavy clusters early to encourage larger individual fruit, and expect the developing crop, not the tree itself, to be the most cold-sensitive stage of the growing cycle.

planting.note: Plant a container-grown tree in spring after frost risk passes, in full sun with well-drained soil; Patillo is a pink-fleshed guava selection grown for its cold tolerance among tropical guava types, useful for Gulf Coast dooryards at the cooler edge of guava range.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after all frost risk has passed; Patillo is a small to medium guava tree valued for bright pink, fragrant flesh with a fruity, tangy-acidic flavor that suits fresh eating, juice, and preserves alike. Pink-fleshed guava selections such as Patillo are generally reported to tolerate cold better and resprout more readily from the roots after a hard freeze than white-fleshed types, a useful trait for gardeners at the northern edge of guava-growing country. As with other guavas, fruit forms on new growth, so an annual late-winter prune keeps the tree compact and encourages a strong flush of fruiting wood each season. Mulch the root zone heavily going into winter, since top growth is more cold-sensitive than the root system and often regrows after being frozen back.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Guava Growing in the Home Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Guava Production Guide

common_name: Thai Lessard Sugar Apple (Ultra-Sweet Green-Skinned Sugar Apple)

planting.note: Transplant grafted or rooted trees into full sun once nights stay reliably above 50°F; Thai Lessard begins bearing at a young age and is among the more cold-tolerant sugar apple selections available, though it still needs a frost-free site or container culture in zone 8.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving this vigorous but manageably sized selection room to branch into a small rounded tree. Thai Lessard is prized for exceptionally sweet, soft, juicy flesh inside its bumpy, pale green skin, and for bearing a heavier and more reliable crop than many older sugar apple selections. It defoliates and drops fruit in cool weather and is killed back by hard frost, so Gulf Coast growers favor a sheltered, south-facing microclimate or keep young trees in containers that can be moved under cover for winter. Hand pollination with a small brush in the early morning, transferring pollen from newly opened male-stage flowers to receptive female-stage flowers, significantly improves fruit set in home gardens where the tree's natural beetle pollinators are absent.
sources: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden Plant Records

planting.note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; atemoya generally needs hand pollination for reliable fruit set in US gardens, since its natural beetle pollinators are absent.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Pinks Mammoth is one of the oldest and most historically significant atemoya cultivars, an early Queensland-bred hybrid known for producing some of the largest fruit of any atemoya selection, occasionally exceeding two pounds, with rich, sweet, custard-white flesh. Cropping tends to be less regular than modern cultivars like Gefner, and fruit can show some irregular shape or blemish, but the exceptional size and flavor keep it popular with home growers chasing a standout specimen fruit. Hand pollination in the morning, moving pollen from male-stage to female-stage flowers, markedly improves fruit set and helps the tree reach its full potential fruit size; harvest as the fruit softens slightly and the skin color lightens, then finish ripening at room temperature.
